source.excerpt: Initially, we examined the feasibility of the targeted synthesis method for the N-propargyl-3-nitropyrrole 4 skeleton starting from pyrrole (1). In the first stage, we applied the mixture of acetic anhydride \mathbf { ( A c _ { 2 } O ) } and nitric acid \mathrm { ( H N O _ { 3 } ) } used in the method reported previously [30] for the nitration of pyrrole. In experiments conducted using this method, both 2-nitro-1H-pyrrole (2) and 3-nitro-1H-pyrrole (3) compounds were formed as a mixture in varying yields. Column chromatography was then used to separate the nitropyrroles from each other. Since we examined 2-nitro-1H-pyrrole (2) and its derivatives in our previous studies [31] and only 3-nitro-1H-pyrrole (3) was found to show dopamin sensor activities [32], we will focus only on 3-nitro-1- H-pyrrole-derived compounds here. After this decision, the reaction was continued using sodium hydride (NaH) in N,N-dimethyl formamide (DMF) to remove the proton attached to the nitrogen atom of the pyrrole and to attach the propargyl group to this nitrogen atom [33], thus giving the target product N-propargyl-3-nitropyrrole (4).

We predicted that an S _ { \mathrm { N } } 2 \cdot -type reaction occurred during the formation of product 4, and performed a theoretical mechanism study to testjerry this prediction, as shown in Fig. 1. The calculations were conducted using the software package Gaussian 09 with the 6-31+g(d) basis set and the B3LYP functional of density functional theory (DFT). The SMD method was chosen as the solvent phase model and DMF was the solvent. To construct the compounds, GaussView 6.0 was used and, to visualize the results, CYLview. Compound 4 with the two proposed TSs was formed. While the TS1 step consists of an acid–base reaction, the S<sub>N</sub>2-type reaction was computationally supported in the TS2 step. The hydride anion of NaH attacked the hydrogen atom of pyrrole in TS1, removing it from the environment and releasing hydrogen gas (H<sub>2</sub>). A free energy of −1.6 kcal/mol was determined for this transition state, indicating a reactant-like TS, and no energy barrier was observed. During the formation of the H⋅⋅⋅HN bond, the distance [d(H⋅⋅⋅HN)] shortened from 1.41 to 1.19 Å, resulting in the S2 intermediate with −25.5 kcal/mol. Here, it is clear that H<sub>2</sub> is separated from the pyrrole moiety and is located at a distance of 3.21 Å. In the continuation of the mechanism, the negatively charged pyrrole unit made a nucleophilic attack on the positively charged propargyl carbon, requiring an energy of 16.2 kcal/mol. It is possible to see the S<sub>N</sub>2-type reaction complex in the relevant image of TS2. Here, it was determined that the N⋅⋅⋅C bond formation began at 2.17 Å, while the C⋅⋅⋅Br bond breakage began at 2.47 Å. As a result, product 4 was formed exergonically with a free energy of −45.5 kcal/mol.

The study continued with the Sonogashira cross-coupling reaction utilized for the derivatization process [34]. Sonogashira coupling is an excellent reaction for attaching an aromatic group to a terminal alkyne [33]. Taking advantage of this feature of the reaction, various aromatic substituents were reacted with N-propargyl-3-nitropyrrole (4) in THF in a basic medium, in the presence of palladium and copper catalysts. After a few halo-substituted aromatic compounds were properly coupled with alkyne 4 to produce compounds 5a–d, the derivatives listed in Table 1 were obtained.

AutoDockTools version 1.5.7 [35] was used in docking of the ligand 4 to the human apoptosis BCL2 (PDB ID: 6O0K; resolution: 1.62 Å), human transferase EGFR (PDB ID: 8A27; resolution: 1.07 Å), and human transferase inhibitor VEGFR (PDB ID: 3VHE; resolution: 1.55 Å). Next, 3D structures of receptors were downloaded from the RCSB Protein Data Bank (RCSB PDB) website and opened with the program Discovery Studio [36] to remove all impurities. Then the receptor chain was saved in PDB format and loaded into the program AutoDock. Here, the Kollman charges were added and saved in PDBQT formats. Ligands were optimized using Gaussian 16 [37] with DFT calculations employing the B3LYP/6–31+G(d) method before being subjected to docking. After setting the grid boxes in xyz dimensions and grid center coordinates for the receptors, the analyses were started (see supplementary material). After completing the in silico molecular docking analyses, the data were subsequently summarized as shown in Table 2. When analyzing the data for BCL2, EGFR, and VEGFR receptors, it was observed that compound 4, which contains two nitro groups, exhibited relatively high affinities, with values of ‒6.26, ‒9.19, and ‒7.72 kcal/mol, respectively. Interestingly, compound 3 showed a better affinity than compound 4 in docking with the BCL2 receptor (−6.70 kcal/mol). However, this result is consistent with the IC₅₀ value in Fig. 2.

The 3-nitro-1H-pyrrole (3) obtained above (800 mg, 7.1 mmol) was taken into a 100-mL beaker. It was dissolved by adding 15 mL of N,Ndimethylformamide (DMF). Then sodium hydride (180 mg, 7.5 mmol) was slowly added to the reaction medium. Gas evolution was observed during this time. It was stirred at room temperature for 10 min. Then propargyl bromide (0.7 mL) was injected with a syringe. The reaction was stirred at room temperature for 24 h. Thin-layer chromatography (TLC) was performed to control the reaction. The crude product was purified by column chromatography. 3-Nitro-1- (prop-2-yn-1-yl)-1H-pyrrole (4) (0.95 g, 6.3 mmol, 89%) was obtained as light-yellow crystals. <sup>1</sup>H NMR (400 MHz, CDCl<sub>3</sub>) δ 7.71–7.66 (m, 1H), 6.76 (dd, J = 3.2, 1.8 Hz, 1H), 6.73–6.70 (m, 1H), 4.74 (d, J = 2.6 Hz, 2H), 2.60 (t, J = 2.6 Hz, 1H); <sup>13</sup>C NMR (100 MHz, CDCl<sub>3</sub>) δ 137.2, 121.4, 121.2, 106.1, 76.0, 75.7, 39.8; IR (ATR, cm<sup>−</sup> <sup>1</sup>) 3260, 3155, 3125, 2963, 2925, 2130, 1669, 1524, 1477, 1376, 1277, 1132, 811, 726; LCMS (Q-TOF) calculated \mathrm { ( C _ { 7 } H _ { 6 } N _ { 2 } O _ { 2 } ) } [M + H]<sup>+</sup>: 151.05021; found 151.04793.
